newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia's Lebed takes first steps on world stage.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed takes first steps on world stage.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed's visit to NATO this week marked a cautious first step onto the world stage and also a key moment in what many see as the "grooming of a president".

The atmosphere after meetings at NATO headquarters in Brussels could best be described as bordering on euphoric. It was enough that he did not rage and wave his finger in anger, that he listened, that he even occasionally smiled.
"He struck us as being very thoughtful," one diplomat said. "Not at all what we were expecting; certainly not a bluff desk-thumping character, but very mild and soft-spoken."
Their fears were understandable. The gravel-voiced former paratroop commander has won a reputation for candour. Before this weekend, he had never set foot in the West.

He has publicly praised former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet's bloody clampdown, compared NATO to a big drunken hooligan in a kindergarten and, only a year ago, warned of a third world war if the alliance expanded eastwards.
This week's Lebed was markedly moderate, criticising growth plans as a threat to Russia but accepting their inevitability.
Diplomats said he started his address to NATO ambassadors by asking them not to judge him by what they read in the press.

Lebed, 46, behaved, by many accounts, as a student might, lowering his booming voice, listening attentively. In as many minutes he described NATO three times as a "strike fist". Secretary-General Javier Solana intoned: "No. An open hand."
"Then I had better change my terminology," Lebed said.

In many ways Western uneasiness about Lebed is reminiscent of trepidation over Boris Yeltsin in the years before he finally ousted Mikhail Gorbachev from power. Yeltsin then, like Lebed now, was viewed by many as unpredictable, a "maverick".

Several capitals were wary of official meetings with him, afraid of undermining Gorbachev. This week, nervous over Yeltsin's impending heart surgery, some had been uncomfortable about the high-level welcome accorded to Lebed, diplomats said.

It was Yeltsin who brought Lebed to the Kremlin as security adviser after the two-star general's strong showing in the summer presidential election. But there are tensions between the two, partly perhaps because of their similarities.
Beyond the booming voice, the rough-hewn looks and evident love of political drama, they share a colourful, forceful style.
Yeltsin has more than once seen fit to slap Lebed down publicly, a humiliation the military man might find galling.
"Lebed is still learning to be a politician, studying to be a president. But it seems to me he's a fast learner," one Russian observer said during Lebed's visit.

Time may be short. The constitution dictates that if Yeltsin, 65, cannot return to duties after surgery, new polls should be called within three months. Lebed could then face strong competition from more experienced politicians such as premier Viktor Chernomyrdin and communist leader Gennady Zyuganov.

In appearance Lebed remains a military figure, just a year after bowing out as commander of the 14th Army in Moldova. His crisp civilian suits sit on him like a uniform and his ramrod bearing at a Brussels news conference, motionless, eyes straight ahead, would have graced any parade ground.
But the army, where he has long been popular, could be a priceless ally at a time of uncertainty.
Lebed's recent clashes with political rivals suggest old ideas of power are not to be abandoned. "If you bang your fist down once on the desk, the question is closed," he once said.
Over two days, Lebed did all that was wanted of him.

Asked if he would shake Lebed's hand for the cameras, NATO European commander General George Joulwan turned directly to his guest. "A handshake? Sure. Maybe we can even make him smile?" Lebed dutifully beamed, for a disconcerting moment every bit the shy and obliging schoolboy at prize-giving.

Lebed, however, is no political upstart but a man with strong political instincts. He used force robustly to quell ethnic conflict in Moldova in 1992 and acted quickly to forge a peace, albeit fragile, in Chechnya.
This week's visit has made him a known face, as well as a known voice, in the West and broad television coverage at home may promote the statesmanlike image he craves there.

When the euphoria subsides, Western officials must weigh the measured tones of this week's guest with the newspaper figure he asked them to disregard. The personal contact has been established but the politician remains essentially an enigma.
Lebed may have been anticipating his own end-of-term report when he told NATO officials after early talks: "A good start."
